A neuromodulator made by midbrain neurons (VTA and substantia nigra). It signals reward prediction errors, shapes learning in the striatum and cortex, and is needed for normal movement.
A neurotransmitter used at the nerve-muscle junction and, in the brain, as a neuromodulator for attention, arousal and plasticity, released from basal forebrain and striatal neurons.
A chemical released by a neuron at a synapse that acts on receptors of the target cell, e.g. glutamate, GABA or dopamine.
A small protein used as a signal between neurons, often released alongside a fast transmitter and acting slowly, e.g. somatostatin or VIP.
A receptor that is itself an ion channel: binding the transmitter opens it within a millisecond, as with AMPA, NMDA and GABA-A receptors.

A receptor that acts through G-proteins and second messengers instead of opening a channel directly. It is slower and longer-lasting, as with GABA-B, dopamine and metabotropic glutamate (mGluR) receptors.

Dopamine acts through two families of receptors: D1-like receptors, which tend to excite and favour potentiation (direct-pathway striatal neurons), and D2-like receptors, which tend to inhibit (indirect-pathway neurons).
An ionotropic acetylcholine receptor, also activated by nicotine. In cortex it excites some interneurons, such as VIP and layer 1 cells.
A small molecule inside a cell, such as calcium, cAMP or IP3, that carries a signal from a receptor to targets inside the cell.
A second messenger made when some metabotropic receptors are activated. It releases calcium from internal stores, which drives calcium waves in astrocytes and some forms of plasticity.
The energy molecule of cells. Released outside cells it also acts as a signal, for example between astrocytes.
Away from synapses: receptors on the membrane outside synapses that respond to transmitter spreading from nearby release, as in volume transmission.
The change in a neuron's membrane potential caused by input at a synapse: excitatory (EPSP) if it depolarizes, inhibitory (IPSP) if it hyperpolarizes.
A brief depolarization of a neuron caused by an excitatory synapse, bringing the membrane potential closer to threshold.
A brief hyperpolarization (or clamp near rest) of a neuron caused by an inhibitory synapse, moving it away from threshold.
The current that flows into a neuron at an excitatory synapse, measured with the voltage held fixed; it causes the EPSP.
A change of the membrane potential toward less negative values, moving the neuron toward its firing threshold.
A change of the membrane potential toward more negative values, moving the neuron away from its firing threshold.
The dip of the membrane potential below rest after a spike, caused by potassium channels. Fast, medium and slow AHPs shape firing rate and adaptation.
The steady membrane potential of a neuron receiving no input, typically around -65 to -70 mV.
The membrane's ability to store charge, like a capacitor, about 1 µF per cm². With membrane resistance it sets how fast the voltage responds to current (the membrane time constant).
How easily current flows through ion channels, the inverse of resistance, measured in siemens. Synaptic and channel conductances change as channels open and close.
How much a neuron's voltage changes for a given injected current. Small neurons and closed channels mean high input resistance.
An ion channel that lets sodium ions into the cell. Fast voltage-gated sodium channels open on depolarization and produce the rising phase of the action potential.
An ion channel that lets potassium ions out of the cell, pulling the voltage back down. The delayed rectifier ends the action potential; other types (A-type, M-type, SK) shape firing.
An ion channel that lets calcium ions into the cell. Voltage-gated calcium channels drive transmitter release, dendritic calcium spikes and bursts, and calcium is a key signal for plasticity.
A small sodium current that does not inactivate. It amplifies inputs near threshold and helps drive subthreshold oscillations and pacemaking.
A fast potassium current that switches on and then inactivates. It delays the first spike and dampens back-propagating spikes in dendrites.
A slow, non-inactivating potassium current through Kv7 (KCNQ) channels, switched off by acetylcholine. It causes spike-frequency adaptation and resonance.
A family of voltage-gated potassium channels that act near threshold, often at the axon initial segment, setting spike threshold and timing.
A small-conductance potassium channel opened by calcium inside the cell. It produces the medium afterhyperpolarization after spikes.

The closing of a channel that stays open-able only after it recovers, even while the voltage still favours opening. Sodium channels inactivate after a spike; T-type calcium channels must be de-inactivated by hyperpolarization before they can fire a burst.
An ion channel that opens or closes as the membrane potential changes, such as the sodium and potassium channels behind the action potential.
A pufferfish toxin that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, used in experiments to stop action potentials.
About the passive spread of voltage along a dendrite or axon, which shrinks and slows with distance like a signal on a leaky cable.
The mathematics of passive voltage spread along dendrites and axons, treating them as leaky electrical cables; the basis of compartmental models.
Inhibition whose reversal potential is near rest, so it barely changes the voltage but opens a leak that divides away excitatory input arriving nearby.
How readily a neuron fires in response to input, set by its channels and membrane properties.
A spike or burst fired just after inhibition ends, because hyperpolarization primed channels such as T-type calcium or HCN.
Having two stable states, e.g. a neuron or network that can stay either quiet or firing until an input switches it.
A regenerative electrical event that starts in a dendrite (sodium, calcium or NMDA spike) instead of at the axon, letting a branch combine its inputs nonlinearly.
Responding strongly only when inputs arrive at almost the same time, as with NMDA receptors or BAC firing in layer 5 cells.
The time between two consecutive spikes of a neuron. The distribution of ISIs shows how regular or bursty the firing is.
The sequence of spike times fired by one neuron.
How many spikes a neuron fires per second (Hz), over a window or averaged across trials.
Tonic firing is steady, ongoing activity; phasic firing is a brief response, such as a burst or pause, to an event.
The study of the electrical activity of neurons, by recording voltages and currents with electrodes.
A recording method in which a glass pipette is sealed onto a neuron's membrane to measure or control its voltage and current very precisely; in whole-cell mode the pipette opens into the cell.
Voltage clamp holds a neuron's voltage fixed and measures the current needed, revealing channel currents. Current clamp injects a set current and measures the voltage.
Recording from two connected neurons at once to measure the synapse between them directly.
The slow voltage recorded by an electrode in brain tissue, summed mostly from synaptic currents of many nearby neurons. Oscillations such as theta and gamma are seen in it.
Recording the brain's electrical activity with electrodes on the scalp; it picks up the summed activity of large populations of cortical neurons.
Brain imaging that tracks changes in blood oxygenation as an indirect, slow measure of neural activity.
Recording the electrical activity of muscles.
Stimulating a patch of cortex through the skull with a brief magnetic pulse from a coil on the head.
Recording neural activity by imaging fluorescent indicators that light up when calcium enters neurons as they fire, often with a two-photon microscope.
Controlling chosen neurons with light by giving them light-sensitive ion channels such as channelrhodopsin.
Imaging with electrons instead of light, sharp enough to see individual synapses; used to reconstruct connectomes.
The molecule a cell copies from its genes to make proteins. Measuring which RNAs a neuron holds (RNA sequencing) shows which genes it uses, the basis of transcriptomic cell types.
In a living animal, as opposed to in a dish or a model.
Outside the living animal, e.g. in a slice of brain tissue kept alive in a dish.
In a computer simulation.
Input that depolarizes a neuron and makes it more likely to fire, usually through glutamate synapses.
Input that makes a neuron less likely to fire, by hyperpolarizing or shunting it, usually through GABA synapses from interneurons.
Activity-dependent change in the strength of synapses, the main way the brain is thought to learn and store memories. Includes LTP, LTD, STDP and short-term plasticity.
A change at synapses that were not themselves active, caused by activity at other synapses on the same cell; it can balance out Hebbian changes.
Plasticity of plasticity: past activity changes how easily a synapse will later potentiate or depress, as in the sliding threshold of the BCM rule.
A connection that carries signals forward through a processing hierarchy, e.g. from thalamus to layer 4, or from a lower to a higher cortical area.
A connection from a higher to a lower stage of a hierarchy, carrying context, expectation or attention; in cortex it often targets layer 1 and the apical dendrites.
A connection between neurons in the same population or layer, so activity can loop and persist.
The local wiring of a small piece of brain, such as one cortical column: which cell types connect to which, and how strongly.
Rhythmic, repeating activity in a group of neurons, seen in the field potential. Named bands include delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma.
Neurons firing at the same moments. Synchrony can make a group's output stronger downstream and may bind features together.
Having only a small fraction of neurons active at a time (or few non-zero connections). Sparse codes are energy-efficient and reduce overlap between patterns.

A state (or set of states) that a dynamical system settles into and returns to after small disturbances. In networks, stored memories can be point attractors and a continuous attractor can hold a position.
A neuron model with no shape: all inputs are summed at one point, as in the LIF model. Contrast multi-compartment models.
Responding strongly to some stimuli and weakly to others, e.g. a V1 neuron preferring one edge orientation.
A layer or simple model that reads a network's activity and turns it into the output, often a trained linear layer.
Two ways a neuron can respond to input: an integrator adds inputs up and fires once enough arrive; a resonator fires best to inputs at its preferred frequency.
How strongly a neuron's output changes for a change in input; the slope of its input-output curve.
A patch of V1 (about 1 mm) holding a full set of orientation columns and ocular dominance columns for one point of the visual field.
The arrangement of cortex into vertical columns of neurons, running through all layers, that share inputs and response properties.
About layers: laminar organization is the arrangement of cortex into layers, and a laminar pattern is how something varies across them.
Memory for specific personal events: what happened, where and when. It depends on the hippocampus.
Holding information in mind for a few seconds to use it, as when remembering a number while dialling.
A fast jump of the eyes from one point to another, several times a second.
Allocentric coordinates are fixed to the world or an object (like a map); egocentric coordinates are relative to the body or a sensor.
About the link between sensing and moving, e.g. how movement changes what is sensed and how sensing guides movement.
Learning rules that use the times of individual spikes, such as STDP, instead of firing rates.

aliases: cells that fire together wire together
definition: Donald Hebb's 1949 idea that when one cell repeatedly helps fire another, the connection between them strengthens; often summed up as cells that fire together wire together.
A sudden qualitative change in a dynamical system's behaviour as a parameter crosses a value, such as a neuron switching from rest to repetitive firing.
A bifurcation where a resting state loses stability and an oscillation appears. Neurons that start firing this way are resonators and begin at a non-zero rate (type II).
A bifurcation where a stable and an unstable state merge and vanish. On an invariant circle (SNIC) it lets a neuron fire at arbitrarily low rates (type I excitability).
In a phase-plane plot, the curve where one variable stops changing. Where nullclines cross is an equilibrium.
A closed loop in state space that a system goes around repeatedly; in a neuron model it is repetitive firing.
Hodgkin's classes of how neurons start firing: type I can fire at any low rate (integrators, often a saddle-node bifurcation); type II jumps to a minimum rate (resonators, often a Hopf bifurcation).
When a system's state depends on its history, e.g. a neuron that starts firing at one current but stops at a lower one.
A system whose state changes over time by fixed rules, usually differential equations; neuron and network models are dynamical systems.
An equation for how a quantity changes over time in terms of its current value, e.g. dV/dt = (−V + RI)/τ for a LIF neuron.
A family of numerical methods that solve differential equations more accurately than Euler steps by sampling the slope several times per step.
An equation for how a probability distribution evolves under drift and noise; used to describe a population of noisy neurons by the distribution of their voltages.
A 1972 rate model of interacting excitatory and inhibitory populations, which shows oscillations and bistability.
A model of short-term synaptic plasticity with a pool of resources that are used up by each spike (depression) and a release probability that rises with use (facilitation).
A random process in which events happen independently at a constant average rate. A standard model of irregular spike trains.
A skewed distribution whose logarithm is normal: most values are small and a few are very large, as with synaptic weights and firing rates in cortex.
How two quantities vary together. Hebbian learning picks up correlations in the input.
A method that finds the directions along which data varies most, used to reduce many neurons' activity to a few dimensions.
A nonlinear method for projecting high-dimensional data (such as population activity) into 2 or 3 dimensions while keeping neighbours close.
A method that extracts smooth low-dimensional trajectories from the spike trains of many neurons recorded at once.

term: Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems
definition: A deep-learning method that fits a recurrent network to recorded spike trains to infer the smooth hidden dynamics behind them, trial by trial.
The number of independent variables needed to describe something, e.g. how many directions population activity really uses.
A filter made by subtracting a wide Gaussian from a narrow one, giving a centre-surround shape like a retinal ganglion cell's receptive field.
An S-shaped function that rises smoothly from 0 to 1, used as a smooth threshold.
A measure of how alike two vectors are: the cosine of the angle between them, from 1 (same direction) to -1.
The straight-line distance between two points.
A network of simple units that output continuous values (not spikes), trained usually by gradient descent; the basis of deep learning.
A neural network that applies small learned filters across an image (convolution), so the same feature detector works everywhere.
A neural network with loops, so its state carries information from earlier inputs; used for sequences.
A recurrent neural network unit with gates that control what to keep, forget and output, letting it remember over long sequences.
The algorithm that trains neural networks by passing the output error backward through the layers to compute each weight's gradient.
Backpropagation applied to a recurrent or spiking network by unrolling it over time steps; used with surrogate gradients to train SNNs.
Training by repeatedly nudging each parameter in the direction that most reduces the error.
The simplest trained neuron model (Rosenblatt, 1958): a weighted sum passed through a threshold, with a rule that adjusts weights after mistakes.
A model that assigns an input to one of a set of categories.
A network trained to reproduce its input through a narrower middle layer, so it learns a compact code.
A learned vector representation of an item (word, image, object) in which similar items are close.
A model that can produce data like what it was trained on, by learning how the data is generated.
A classic dataset of 70,000 small images of handwritten digits, 0 to 9, used as a first test for classifiers, including SNNs.
A neuromorphic version of MNIST, recorded by moving an event camera in front of the digits so each image becomes a stream of spikes.
A LIF neuron whose threshold rises after each spike and decays back, giving spike-frequency adaptation and a longer memory.

term: Long Short-Term Memory Spiking Neural Network
definition: A recurrent SNN that mixes ordinary LIF neurons with adaptive (ALIF) ones, so it can hold information over seconds (Bellec et al., 2018).
A learning rule for recurrent SNNs (Bellec et al., 2020) that approximates BPTT with local eligibility traces multiplied by a learning signal broadcast to each neuron.
A surrogate-gradient learning rule for multi-layer SNNs (Zenke and Ganguli, 2018) built from local traces and a feedback error signal.
A method and library for training SNNs with backpropagation that assigns error back through time and across layers (Shrestha and Orchard, 2018).
Nengo's online learning rule: it changes decoder weights in proportion to an error signal times each neuron's activity, a supervised delta rule for spiking networks.
A recurrent network of binary neurons that combines STDP, synaptic normalisation and intrinsic plasticity and learns to predict input sequences (Lazar et al., 2009).
Training an ordinary neural network and then translating it into a spiking network with matching firing rates, instead of training the SNN directly.
A bridge that runs Brian2 models on GPUs through the GeNN code generator.
A Brian2 back end that generates CUDA code to run simulations on NVIDIA GPUs.
The Python interface to the NEST simulator.
A modelling language for writing new neuron and synapse models for the NEST simulator.
A widely used simulator for detailed, multi-compartment neuron models; CoreNEURON is its optimised engine for large models.
A standard XML-based language for describing neuron and network models so they can be shared between simulators.
A PyTorch-based library for training deep spiking neural networks.
A PyTorch-based Python library for simulating SNNs, aimed at machine-learning experiments with STDP and similar rules.
Add-ons to Nengo: NengoDL runs and trains Nengo models with TensorFlow; NengoLoihi runs them on Intel's Loihi chip.
The deep-learning library of Intel's Lava framework, for training SNNs that can run on Loihi.
The software that runs PyNN models on SpiNNaker hardware.
The Python interface to the GeNN GPU code generator.
A widely used Python library for deep learning with automatic gradients and GPU support; many SNN libraries build on it.
Google's deep-learning library.
Google's Python library for fast array maths with automatic gradients, compiled for CPUs, GPUs and TPUs.
The standard Python library for fast numerical arrays.
A commercial numerical computing environment and language, common in neuroscience labs.
NVIDIA's platform for programming its GPUs for general computation.
A processor with thousands of simple cores that run the same operation in parallel; used for deep learning and large simulations.
The general-purpose processor of a computer, with a few fast cores.
The set of functions and rules a library or service offers to programs that use it.
A standard for programs running on many computers or cores to exchange messages; NEST uses it to spread large simulations across a cluster.
Running large computations on supercomputers or clusters of many processors.
A chip designed for one purpose, such as a neuromorphic processor, rather than general computing.
Building integrated circuits with millions or billions of transistors on one chip. Mead's analog VLSI started neuromorphic engineering.
Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, the transistor technology used for almost all modern chips.
Fully depleted silicon-on-insulator, a chip process with a thin insulating layer that lowers power; used for SpiNNaker2.
A single chip that holds a whole computer: processors, memory controllers and interfaces.
A small packet-switched network inside a chip that carries messages between its cores, as in neuromorphic chips sending spikes.
Fast on-chip memory that keeps its data while powered, without refreshing; neuromorphic chips store synapses in it.
Dense, cheaper memory that must be refreshed constantly; the main memory of computers. SDRAM is synchronous DRAM.
Memory a processor can read or write at any address in about the same time.
Small blocks of dedicated memory inside an FPGA.
In an FPGA, a small memory that implements any logic function of a few inputs; the basic building block of its logic.
A dedicated multiply-accumulate unit inside an FPGA; also digital signal processing in general.
A description of a digital circuit as registers and the logic between them, written in a hardware language such as VHDL or Verilog.
A hardware description language for designing digital circuits such as FPGA designs (Verilog is the other common one).
A kind of parallelism where one instruction acts on many data values at once, as in vector units.
The operation a = a + w × x, the core step of neural-network computation.
Representing numbers as integers with an implied decimal point; cheaper in hardware than floating point but with limited range and precision.
Representing numbers with a mantissa and exponent, giving wide range; standard on CPUs and GPUs.
The lowest-value bit of a binary number.
A family of low-power processor designs. SpiNNaker uses ARM968 cores and SpiNNaker2 uses ARM Cortex-M4F cores.
The processor architecture of most desktop and server computers (Intel and AMD).
Hertz (Hz) counts cycles per second; a megahertz is a million per second. Firing rates are given in Hz, clock speeds in MHz or GHz.
A circuit element whose resistance depends on the current that has passed through it, so it can store a synaptic weight; arranged in crossbar arrays it can do multiply-accumulate in place.
A commercial neuromorphic processor from BrainChip for low-power, event-based inference.
A company making small low-power neuromorphic chips for event-based vision and audio.
IBM's 2023 inference chip, a successor to TrueNorth that keeps memory beside compute but uses low-precision ordinary (non-spiking) neural networks.
The US defence research agency; its SyNAPSE program funded IBM's TrueNorth.
The computer company whose research lab built the TrueNorth and NorthPole chips.
A family of digital logic, and by extension its signal levels: about 0 V for low and 5 V (or 3.3 V) for high.
Red, green and blue, the three colour channels a display mixes to make every colour. VGA carries each as a separate analog signal.
A circuit that turns a digital number into a voltage; a VGA output uses one per colour channel.
A circuit that measures a voltage and turns it into a digital number.
The data wire of an I2C bus.
The clock wire of an I2C bus.
The industry group that publishes display standards, including the VGA timing tables (DMT) and DisplayPort.
VESA's standard list of display modes and their exact timings: pixel clock, porches and sync widths for each resolution and refresh rate.
The old display tube that draws the picture by sweeping an electron beam across a phosphor screen line by line; VGA timing comes from it.
A digital audio and video connection standard, successor to DVI for TVs and monitors.
A digital video connection, between VGA and HDMI, that uses TMDS signalling.
A VESA digital video standard that sends data in packets.
The encoding DVI and HDMI use to send pixel data over differential pairs with few bit transitions and balanced DC.
The standard connector and protocol for attaching devices to computers.
How many times per second a display draws a full frame, e.g. 60 Hz.
The number of pixels a display shows, width by height, e.g. 640 × 480 for standard VGA.

term: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: A professional association for engineering that publishes many journals and runs conferences, including several on neural networks and circuits.

term: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
definition: A major US general-science journal.
A publisher of open-access journals, including PLoS Computational Biology and PLoS ONE.

term: Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
definition: A leading yearly machine-learning conference.
A leading yearly machine-learning conference.
A leading yearly deep-learning conference.

term: International Joint Conference on Neural Networks
definition: A yearly conference on neural networks, run by IEEE and the International Neural Network Society.

term: IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems
definition: A yearly conference on circuit design, including neuromorphic circuits.
A leading yearly conference on computer architecture.

term: Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
definition: A leading yearly computer-vision conference.
A leading computer-vision conference, held every two years.
An open-access journal for the life sciences and biomedicine.
A paper shared publicly before peer review, on a server such as arXiv or bioRxiv.
The Swiss university in Lausanne that hosted the Blue Brain Project.
A US university; MIT Press publishes many computational neuroscience books.

A set of free licences for sharing creative work. CC BY lets anyone reuse the work if they credit the author; BY-SA adds that changed versions must use the same licence; CC0 gives the work to the public domain.
Work that no one owns the copyright to, so anyone may use it freely.
Software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, change and share it.
A free online repository of openly licensed images and media, used by Wikipedia.
A lossless image file format.
A common lossy image file format for photos.
An image format that describes drawings as shapes and lines, so they stay sharp at any size.
The programming language of web pages; this library's simulations are written in it.
A plain-text format for structured data; this library stores its pages and terms in JSON files.
Retinal and thalamic cells that respond to light increments (ON cells) or decrements (OFF cells) in the centre of their receptive field. ON-OFF cells respond to both.
A class of layer 5/6 pyramidal cell whose axon stays mostly near home, with few long-range targets; a smaller group beside IT, ET and CT cells.
In the Thousand Brains Project's Monty, a sensor module turns raw sensor data into features at a location and sends them to learning modules in the Cortical Messaging Protocol.

Touch nerve fibres from the skin, grouped by how they adapt to steady pressure: slowly adapting type 1 (SA1, Merkel cells, fine shape), rapidly adapting (RA or FA1, Meissner corpuscles, flutter and slip), SA2 (Ruffini endings, skin stretch) and Pacinian (PC or FA2, vibration).

NMDA receptors are built from an NR1 (GluN1) subunit and NR2 (GluN2) subunits. NR2A-containing receptors are faster; NR2B-containing ones are slower and more common early in development; the mix changes how plasticity works.
The chemical that gives the NMDA receptor its name; it activates that receptor and no other glutamate receptor.
The sleep stage with vivid dreams, fast eye movements, a waking-like EEG and limp muscles, when the hippocampus shows theta rhythm.
Deep non-REM sleep, with large slow oscillations, up and down states, sleep spindles and sharp-wave ripples, thought to help consolidate memory.
A model of the basal ganglia where the direct pathway says go (release an action) and the indirect pathway says no-go (suppress it); dopamine shifts the balance.
A pump that moves calcium from the cell's interior back into internal stores (the endoplasmic reticulum), ending calcium signals.
A glutamate transporter found in some unusual cells, such as a group of CCK basket cells and cochlear inner hair cells; used as a cell-type marker.
A transcription factor gene that marks corticothalamic layer 6 neurons in mouse cortex.
An ionotropic serotonin receptor. In cortex it marks the group of interneurons (including VIP and neurogliaform cells) born in the caudal ganglionic eminence.
Receptors for serotonin (5-HT). 5-HT1A receptors usually inhibit, 5-HT2A receptors usually excite (and are the target of psychedelics), and 5-HT3 receptors are fast ion channels.
A Blue Brain morphological type: a pyramidal cell whose apical dendrite ends in a tuft in layer 1 (TPC:A, TPC:B, TPC:C for different shapes).
How many times faster a process runs for a 10 °C rise in temperature; channel rates in the Hodgkin-Huxley model scale with Q10 of about 3.
A plot of the current through a membrane or channel against the voltage across it, used to find reversal potentials and nonlinearities.
The family of neuron models that sum input in their membrane potential and fire a spike when it crosses a threshold, then reset, such as the LIF model.
A constant current, as opposed to an alternating or fluctuating one; in simulations, a steady input injected into neurons.
A 2021 proposal by Geoffrey Hinton for a neural network that represents part-whole hierarchies with columns of embeddings that agree at each level, an idea close to column voting.
A neural network (Sabour, Frosst and Hinton, 2017) whose groups of neurons (capsules) encode an object part and its pose, and agree by routing on the whole object.
Machine Intelligence from Cortical Networks: a project that imaged the activity of a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex and then mapped its wiring with electron microscopy.
The US Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies initiative. Its cell census networks (BICCN, then BICAN) catalogue the brain's cell types.
A public database of tens of thousands of digitally reconstructed neuron shapes.
An international organisation that promotes shared standards and tools for neuroscience data, such as NeuroML.
In the insect antennal lobe, an interneuron that connects glomeruli locally; also in this library, LN can mean the linear-nonlinear model.
A continuous attractor network whose neurons lie on a ring, with nearby neurons exciting each other (connectivity J0 + J1 cos(Δθ)), so a bump of activity can hold a direction or angle.

The table of connection strengths between populations. Names such as wEE, wEI and wIE give the weight between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations, with the two letters naming the populations it joins; check each page for which letter is the target.
A unit of memory size: about a million bytes (a byte is 8 bits). kB is a thousand bytes, GB a billion; kbit and Mbit count bits.
Razavi's picture of the eight mutually trading specifications of an analog circuit: gain, bandwidth, power, supply voltage, linearity, noise, swing and impedance.
Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: a voltage-controlled device whose gate voltage forms a conducting channel between source and drain.
The gate-source voltage (VTH) at which a MOS transistor's channel begins to form and appreciable current flows.
VGS minus VTH: how far the gate is above threshold. It sets the drain current, the transconductance and the minimum VDS needed for saturation.
The small-signal ratio of output current change to input voltage change; for a MOSFET gm = dID/dVGS = 2ID/Vov in saturation.
The region (VDS < Vov) where a MOSFET behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.
The region (VDS >= Vov) where a MOSFET's channel is pinched off and the drain current is nearly independent of VDS; the normal operating region of analog amplifiers.
The rise in a MOSFET's threshold voltage when its source is at a higher voltage than its bulk (VSB > 0).
The shortening of the effective channel as VDS rises in saturation, which makes drain current grow slightly with VDS and gives the transistor a finite output resistance.
The exponentially small drain current that flows below threshold; also called weak inversion. It offers the highest gm per unit current.
The product gm*ro of a transistor: the largest voltage gain obtainable from one device, equal to 2/(lambda*Vov).
The small-signal resistance seen looking into a transistor's drain; ro = 1/(lambda*ID) in saturation.
The frequency at which a transistor's small-signal current gain drops to unity: fT = gm / (2*pi*(Cgs + Cgd)).
The apparent multiplication of a capacitance bridging the input and output of an inverting amplifier by (1 + gain) as seen from the input.
The basic MOS voltage amplifier: input at the gate, output at the drain, source at the AC ground. Small-signal gain is -gm*(RD || ro).
A resistance in series with the source that trades gain for linearity: transconductance becomes gm/(1+gm*RS).
A transistor with gate shorted to drain, which behaves like a nonlinear resistance of about 1/gm.
A common-drain amplifier with gain just below one, high input impedance and low output impedance (1/gm); used as a voltage buffer and level shifter.
An amplifier with signal at the source and output at the drain; low input resistance (about 1/gm), non-inverting.
A stack of a common-gate transistor on a common-source transistor that raises output resistance to about gm*ro^2 and gain to about (gm*ro)^2, at the cost of headroom.
A cascode whose upper device has the opposite polarity, so the signal current is folded to the other supply rail, saving voltage headroom.
A simplification for symmetric differential circuits: analyse one side with the symmetry axis treated as AC ground.
The ratio of a differential amplifier's differential gain to its common-mode-to-differential gain; a measure of how well it rejects common-mode interference.
How a differential circuit reacts to a signal applied equally to both inputs.
A multiplier made from stacked differential pairs whose output current is proportional to the product of two differential inputs; used as a mixer.
A circuit that copies a reference current to another branch by sharing the gate-source voltage of matched transistors.
An amplifier whose output is a current proportional to the differential input voltage; the five-transistor OTA is the simplest CMOS example.
A transistor used as a load, often a current mirror, giving high small-signal resistance with a small voltage drop.
Setting a transistor's DC operating point, usually via a current mirror from a stable reference.
The pole closest to the origin, which determines the bandwidth of an amplifier or the speed of a feedback system's response.
For a one-pole amplifier, the product of low-frequency gain and -3 dB bandwidth; it equals the unity-gain frequency.
Random voltage or current noise from the thermal motion of charge carriers; white, with PSD 4kTR for a resistor.
Low-frequency noise whose power density rises as 1/f, caused by traps at the gate-oxide interface; falls with larger device area.
The total thermal noise voltage on a capacitor, sqrt(kT/C), independent of the resistance that charges it.
Noise power per unit bandwidth, in V^2/Hz or A^2/Hz.
The noise voltage or current, placed at an amplifier's input, that would produce the same output noise from a noiseless amplifier.
The width of an ideal brick-wall filter that passes the same total noise power as the real circuit (pi/2 times the pole frequency for one pole).
The product A*beta around a feedback loop; the closed-loop gain is A/(1 + loop gain).
The reduction by (1 + loop gain) in the sensitivity of a closed-loop amplifier's gain to variations in the open-loop gain.
A shunt-shunt feedback amplifier whose output voltage is proportional to the input current; low input and output resistance.
An expression for a feedback circuit's port impedance: Z = Z0*(1 + T_sc)/(1 + T_oc), with T_sc and T_oc the loop gains with the port shorted or open.
A high-gain differential amplifier meant to be used with negative feedback.
A single-stage op amp where the input pair and cascode devices are the same polarity, giving the highest gain and lowest noise but the smallest swing.
The maximum rate of change of an amplifier's output, limited by the current available to charge a capacitor (SR = I/C).
Using an auxiliary amplifier to regulate a cascode device and so multiply the output resistance (and gain) without costing voltage headroom.
A loop that senses the average output voltage of a fully differential amplifier and adjusts bias currents to keep it at a set value.
The differential input voltage needed to bring an amplifier's output to zero, caused by device mismatch.
A measure of how well an amplifier ignores variations on the supply voltage.
The amount by which the loop-gain phase is above -180 degrees at the frequency where its magnitude is 1; a measure of stability.
A feedback loop oscillates at a frequency where the loop gain has magnitude one and phase -180 degrees.
Adding capacitors or other elements to an amplifier so that its loop gain falls through 0 dB with enough phase margin.
The effect of Miller compensation in a two-stage amplifier: the first pole moves to lower frequency and the second to higher.
Compensating a two-stage op amp with a capacitor around the second stage, using the Miller effect to create a large dominant-pole capacitance.
A resistor in series with the Miller capacitor that moves the right-half-plane zero to infinity or into the left half plane.
A design approach that uses the ratio of transconductance to drain current as the main sizing variable, valid from weak to strong inversion.
A voltage reference that sums a CTAT base-emitter voltage and a scaled PTAT voltage to cancel temperature dependence, giving about 1.2 V.
Proportional to absolute temperature: a voltage or current that rises linearly with temperature, such as VT*ln(n).
Complementary to absolute temperature: a voltage that falls with temperature, such as a base-emitter voltage.
The error charge a MOS switch deposits on its load capacitor when it turns off, from its channel charge being expelled.
Output components at integer multiples of the input frequency created by a nonlinear circuit.
Mixing of two or more input tones in a nonlinear circuit to produce sum and difference frequencies.
Random differences between nominally identical devices, falling as 1/sqrt(area) (Pelgrom's law).
An odd number of inverters connected in a loop, oscillating with period 2*N*Td.
An oscillator whose frequency is set by a control voltage: w_out = w0 + K_VCO*V_cont.
Short-term random fluctuation of an oscillator's phase, seen as spectral skirts around the carrier.
A feedback system that makes an oscillator's phase track a reference, used for clock generation and frequency synthesis.
A circuit that sources or sinks a current into a capacitor in proportion to the phase error; the output stage of a PLL phase detector.
A feedback loop that aligns a clock with a delayed copy by adjusting a delay line rather than an oscillator.
A simulation condition representing the extremes of process variation (for example fast-fast or slow-slow) that a circuit must tolerate.
The limit on carrier speed at high electric field that makes short-channel drain current rise linearly, not quadratically, with overdrive.
A short-channel effect in which the drain voltage lowers the source-channel barrier, reducing VTH and output resistance.
A failure in which a parasitic thyristor in a CMOS structure turns on and shorts the supply to ground.
The patterning step that transfers a mask pattern into light-sensitive resist on a wafer.
Doping a semiconductor by shooting accelerated dopant ions into it.
A layout technique that arranges matched devices symmetrically about a common centre so linear process gradients cancel.
A grounded or biased ring around a circuit that collects substrate currents and isolates it from noise or latch-up.
A MOSFET whose channel carries electrons: it turns on when the gate is raised above the source by more than the threshold voltage.

A MOSFET whose channel carries holes: it turns on when the gate is pulled below the source by more than the magnitude of its threshold voltage. Holes are slower than electrons, so it needs about 2 to 4 times the W/L of an NMOS for the same current.
The voltage across the base-emitter junction of a bipolar transistor. At fixed current it falls by about 2 mV per kelvin, which makes it a CTAT quantity used in bandgap references.

A PLL block that compares the reference and feedback clocks and outputs pulses whose width is the phase error. Unlike a plain phase detector it also tells which clock is faster, so the loop can lock from any starting frequency.
A circuit whose output is proportional to the phase difference between two signals; it is the comparison element of a PLL.
The low-pass filter (often a resistor and capacitors) between the charge pump and the VCO. It averages the pulses into a control voltage and sets the loop's dynamics and bandwidth.
A circuit that outputs a clock whose frequency is the input frequency divided by an integer N. In a PLL it lets the output run at N times the reference frequency.
A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates frequencies above its cutoff, such as an RC network.
A fabrication step that etches shallow trenches around each transistor and fills them with oxide to isolate neighbouring devices. It is the modern replacement for LOCOS.
An older isolation technique that grows thick oxide between active areas. Its bulging edge, the bird's beak, wastes area, which is why shallow trench isolation replaced it.
A family of industry-standard compact MOSFET models used in SPICE simulation. It includes short-channel effects, so it is far more accurate than the square-law equations.
A four-layer p-n-p-n structure that, once triggered, latches on and conducts a large current. It is the parasitic path behind latch-up in CMOS and is also used deliberately in ESD protection.
The input (IIP3) or output (OIP3) level at which the extrapolated third-order intermodulation product would equal the fundamental. A higher value means a more linear circuit.
A process that puts bipolar and CMOS transistors on one chip, combining the high gain and low noise of bipolars with CMOS density.
A bipolar transistor with an n-type emitter and collector and a p-type base. It conducts when the base is about 0.7 V above the emitter.
A bipolar transistor with a p-type emitter and collector and an n-type base. Standard CMOS processes offer a parasitic vertical PNP, which bandgap circuits use.
A three-terminal device, with emitter, base and collector, whose collector current is set exponentially by the base-emitter voltage.
The operating region where VGS is below the threshold voltage and the channel is off, apart from a small subthreshold leakage current.
A linear equivalent circuit that describes how small changes around a bias point behave. For a MOSFET it consists of the current source gm*vgs, the resistance ro and the capacitances.
The current source that joins the sources of a differential pair and sets the total current the pair shares.
The part of a pair of signals that is the same on both: the average of the two. A differential amplifier ideally ignores it.
The difference between the two signals of a pair, which a differential amplifier amplifies.
How much the loop gain could rise at the frequency where the phase reaches -180 degrees before the loop starts to oscillate. It is measured in dB.
The frequency at which the gain magnitude falls to 1 (0 dB). The phase margin is measured here.

A frequency at which a transfer function's numerator is zero so the gain rises toward it by 20 dB per decade. Zeros often come from a signal path that bypasses the amplifier, such as a feedforward capacitor.
A zero that adds phase lag instead of lead while raising the gain. It appears in Miller-compensated stages and can be cancelled with a series resistor.
The fraction of the output fed back to the input in a feedback loop, usually written beta. The loop gain is A*beta.
The gain of an amplifier with feedback applied: Af = A / (1 + A*beta). For a large loop gain it approaches 1/beta.
The gain of an amplifier with no feedback applied.
Noise from the random arrival of charge carriers crossing a barrier such as a pn junction, with mean square current 2*q*I*df.
A measure of the noise a circuit adds, in dB: the ratio of the input signal-to-noise ratio to the output signal-to-noise ratio. A noiseless circuit has 0 dB.
The frequency where two behaviours meet. For noise, it is where flicker noise falls to the level of thermal noise; for a filter, where the gain is 3 dB down.
The ratio of the power in all harmonics of a tone to the power in the fundamental, a measure of nonlinearity.
The input level at which an amplifier's gain has dropped by 1 dB from its small-signal value because of nonlinearity.
The ratio of the largest signal a circuit can handle with acceptable distortion to the smallest signal it can resolve above its noise.
The ratio of the signal level to the strongest unwanted spur or distortion product. It is a common figure for converters and amplifiers.
An oscillator built around an inductor-capacitor resonator. It has lower phase noise than a ring oscillator but needs an inductor and more area.
A capacitor whose value changes with the voltage across it, often a reverse-biased pn junction or MOS device. It tunes the frequency of a VCO.
A parallel inductor and capacitor that resonates at 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)). Its losses are modelled by a parallel resistance Rp.
A measure of how little energy a resonator loses per cycle: the ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle, times 2*pi. A higher Q means a sharper resonance and lower phase noise.
The random variation of a clock's edges from their ideal times. It is the time-domain view of phase noise.
The range of input frequencies over which a PLL can stay locked, or in which it locks quickly without cycle slipping.
The range of input frequencies from which an unlocked PLL can acquire lock.
The frequency range over which a PLL tracks its input. A wider loop follows the reference more closely, while a narrower one filters the reference noise more.
A transistor that connects a signal to a capacitor while the clock is high and isolates it when the clock is low. Its on-resistance and the capacitor set the sampling bandwidth.
An NMOS and a PMOS in parallel, driven by opposite clocks. It keeps the on-resistance low over the whole signal range.
A circuit that uses switches and capacitors, instead of resistors, to process signals in discrete time; the effective resistance of a capacitor switched at fclk is 1/(fclk*C).
A circuit that follows an input (track mode) and then freezes its value on a capacitor (hold mode), giving a converter a steady value to measure.
The error when a signal is sampled at less than twice its highest frequency: higher frequencies fold back and appear as lower ones.
The operating regime where VGS is well above threshold, the channel is fully formed and the current follows the square law.
The transition regime between weak and strong inversion, where neither the exponential nor the square-law model is accurate.
A normalized measure of how strongly a transistor is inverted, used to choose a bias point between weak and strong inversion.
Damage caused by carriers accelerated by a high electric field near the drain; they enter the oxide and shift the threshold voltage over time.
A layout technique that splits two matched transistors into interleaved fingers so that gradients across the chip affect both equally.
An unused device placed at the edge of a matched group so the active ones see the same surroundings and etch behaviour.
Damage to a thin gate oxide caused by charge collected on a long metal line that is connected to it during fabrication.
The thin insulating layer between the gate and the channel. Its thickness sets the gate capacitance Cox.
Polycrystalline silicon, used for the gate electrode and for resistors.
A lightly n-doped region in a p-type substrate that holds PMOS transistors.
A lightly p-doped region in an n-type substrate that holds NMOS transistors.
The silicon wafer in which the transistors are built. The substrate terminal of a MOSFET is also called the body or bulk.
A region around a pn junction or under a MOS gate that has been emptied of free carriers, leaving fixed charge.
The boundary between p-type and n-type semiconductor, which conducts in one direction.
A two-terminal device that conducts current in one direction. Its current rises exponentially with forward voltage.
One terminal of a bipolar transistor. It supplies the carriers and carries the sum of base and collector current.
The terminal of a bipolar transistor that collects the carriers. Its current is set by the base-emitter voltage.
The increase of bipolar collector current with collector-emitter voltage because the base narrows. It plays the role channel-length modulation plays in a MOSFET.
A logarithmic unit for ratios. For voltage or current gain, dB = 20*log10(ratio); for power, 10*log10(ratio).
A graph of a transfer function's magnitude in dB and its phase against frequency on a logarithmic axis.
The ratio of a circuit's output to its input as a function of frequency; its poles and zeros determine the frequency response.
The impedance seen looking into an amplifier's input, which determines how much it loads the source.
The impedance seen looking into an amplifier's output, which determines how much the load reduces the gain.
The ratio of output voltage to input voltage of an amplifier.
The ratio of output current to input current of an amplifier.
The range of frequencies over which a circuit's gain stays within 3 dB of its low-frequency value.
The time an output takes to get within a specified error band of its final value after a step.
The capacitance an amplifier drives at its output. It sets the output pole and the amplifier's bandwidth and speed.
The DC current that sets the operating point of a transistor and with it gm, ro and the swing.
The supply voltage left over after the minimum voltages the transistors in a stack need to stay in saturation; it limits the output swing.
The range over which the output can move while every transistor stays in its intended region.
The range of input common-mode voltages over which an amplifier works properly, with the input pair and the tail source in saturation.
A circuit that supplies a nearly constant current regardless of the voltage across it. A transistor in saturation approximates one.
A voltage regulator that keeps its output constant even when the input is only slightly above it, built from a pass transistor and a feedback amplifier.
An amplifier whose input or output can swing nearly the full range between the supplies.
An output stage in which both transistors conduct a little around zero signal and one takes over at larger swings. It drives heavy loads with low standby current.
An extra amplifier that senses a cascode device's source and adjusts its gate to raise the output resistance further, at the cost of power.
The bandwidth of an ideal brick-wall filter that would pass the same noise power as a real filter of unity peak gain. For a first-order low-pass filter it is (pi/2) times the -3 dB frequency.
Sampling a signal much faster than the Nyquist rate so quantization noise is spread over a wider band and can be filtered out.
A converter's resolution as measured from its real signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, usually lower than its nominal bit count.
The deviation of each step of a converter from the ideal 1 LSB step.
The maximum deviation of a converter's transfer curve from a straight line.
A circuit that multiplies two signals, so frequencies add and subtract. It moves a signal from one frequency to another, as in the Gilbert cell.
The first amplifier in a receiver, designed to add as little noise as possible so the weak input signal is not buried.
Frequencies from a few kilohertz up to hundreds of gigahertz used for wireless communication.
A circuit chain that picks up a weak radio signal and converts it to a usable one; its first blocks are usually an LNA and a mixer.
A physical constant, 1.38e-23 J/K, that links temperature to energy. It appears in thermal noise: 4kT*R.
How easily carriers move under an electric field. A higher mobility gives a higher current for a given W/L; electrons are about 2 to 4 times as mobile as holes.
The gate capacitance per unit area, equal to the oxide permittivity divided by the oxide thickness.
The ratio of a transistor's channel width to its length. The current at a given bias is proportional to it.
A wide transistor split into several narrow gate fingers connected in parallel, which reduces gate resistance and junction capacitance.
Unwanted capacitance between wires and devices that the designer didn't draw but the layout creates.
The capacitance of a reverse-biased pn junction, such as the drain-to-body junction of a MOSFET, which falls as the reverse bias rises.
The capacitance between the gate and the source or drain regions that extend slightly under it.
The capacitance between gate and source, about (2/3)*W*L*Cox in saturation plus overlap.
The capacitance between gate and drain. It bridges input and output in a common-source stage and is multiplied by the Miller effect.
A sudden transfer of charge between objects at different voltages, which can destroy thin gate oxides. Pads include protection structures to divert it.
Variations in process, supply voltage and temperature, which a design must tolerate.
How much a quantity changes per degree of temperature, for example in ppm per degree.
A simulation repeated many times with random device variations, to see the statistical spread of a circuit's performance.
The standard circuit simulator, which solves a netlist of devices for its DC, AC and transient behaviour.
A node held at a fixed voltage by feedback without being connected to a fixed supply, such as the inverting input of an op amp with feedback.
An op-amp circuit with the input applied through a resistor to the inverting input. The gain is -R2/R1.
An op-amp circuit with the signal applied to the non-inverting input. The gain is 1 + R2/R1.
A circuit that outputs a logic high or low depending on whether one input is larger than the other. It is a high-gain amplifier or a regenerative latch.
A comparator with hysteresis: it switches at a higher threshold on the way up than on the way down, which stops noise from causing false transitions.
Positive feedback that amplifies a small difference quickly until it reaches full logic levels, as in a latch.
The time between a change at a gate's input and the resulting change at its output. It sets the frequency of a ring oscillator.
The number of gate inputs a single output drives. FO4 delay (an inverter driving four copies of itself) is a technology-independent speed measure.
A circuit that has been reduced to a voltage source in series with a resistance (or, as the Norton form, a current source in parallel).
Two rules for circuits: currents entering a node sum to zero (KCL), and voltages around a loop sum to zero (KVL).
